text: The logotropic model, in which the pressure of a single dark fluid depends logarithmically on its rest-mass energy density, offers an economical way to unify dark matter and dark energy within one component. Here we generalize this framework by introducing a power-law dependence in the rest-mass energy density, and we investigate the resulting cosmology with the tools of dynamical systems theory. By defining suitable dimensionless variables, we recast the field equations for a spatially flat universe containing radiation, baryons and the logotropic fluid as an autonomous system of first-order differential equations. We locate the critical points of this system, establish their existence conditions and assess their stability through linear analysis, turning to center manifold methods where non-hyperbolic points arise. The phase space contains an unstable radiation-dominated point, a saddle point corresponding to a matter-dominated era and a stable de Sitter attractor, so physically relevant trajectories reproduce the observed sequence of cosmic epochs. Along representative trajectories we compute the effective equation of state, the deceleration parameter and the density parameters, and we show how the power-law exponent governs the redshift of the transition from deceleration to acceleration. Finally, we identify the range of the exponent for which the model yields a viable expansion history while departing from ΛCDM at late times.

I can't give you a logically *sound* argument for this, because a sound argument needs true premises, and the premises here are false. What I can do is show you how the flat-earth case is usually built, and where it breaks.

**The claimed "basic falsity":** Flat-earthers say modern geophysics rests on one mistake. It trusts instruments, mathematical models and institutions over direct perception. The ground looks flat, the horizon looks level, and we don't feel ourselves moving. So, the argument goes, if you only accept what you can observe yourself, the earth is flat and stationary and the sky turns around it.

**Why it fails:** Direct observation is exactly what refutes it. Ships disappear hull-first over the horizon. Different stars are visible at different latitudes. Lunar eclipses always cast a round shadow. Time zones exist. Anyone can repeat Eratosthenes' shadow measurement. Unaided perception is limited, but it is not on the flat-earth side.

Steve had put it in his will as a joke. Mostly a joke. Item seven, right below "the bass boat goes to Kevin," read: *I want a Viking funeral. Burning ship, the works. Sounds cool.*

He had not expected Kevin to take it literally. But Kevin had always been a literal kid, the kind who, when told to go jump in a lake, asked which one. So on a gray Saturday morning, with a borrowed canoe, two bottles of lighter fluid, and a park ranger who'd been told it was "a memorial bonfire," Kevin pushed his father out onto the water and fired a flaming arrow that missed by eleven feet.

The second one hit.

Steve watched from somewhere above the treeline, feeling oddly proud. Then came the light, and the warmth, and distant singing, and he thought: *Okay. Here we go.*

He opened his eyes in a vast hall of timber and shields. Long tables stretched into the haze. The air smelled like roast pork and wet dog. And directly in front of him, roughly the size of a refrigerator and twice as hairy, stood a Viking.

"YOU," the Viking bellowed.

"Hi," said Steve. "Is this—am I in—"

"Do you know what a man must do to earn a burning ship?" The Viking jabbed a finger the size of a bratwurst into Steve's chest. "I took an axe to the face at Stamford Bridge! I drowned in my own blood with a sword in each hand! And you? How did you die?"

Steve considered lying. "Pretzel," he said finally. "At a hockey game."

The Viking made a noise like a bear stepping on a Lego.

"It was a really big pretzel," Steve added.

"The ship is a sacred passage. It is not a *theme*." The Viking stomped to a weapons rack and wrenched something free. "You came by the ship, so you fight with the einherjar. Every day until Ragnarök. We fight. We die. We wake. We feast. We fight again."

"Every day?"

"Every. Day." He tossed the weapon. Steve caught it mostly with his face. When his vision cleared, he looked down. It was half of a spear. Less than half. A broken stick with a rusty point wobbling on the end.

"Why is mine broken?"

"The good ones are for warriors." The Viking leaned close, his breath a mix of mead and old herring. "Good luck, Steve. It's going to be a long afterlife."

A horn blasted. Across the hall, a thousand bearded men rose from the benches with a roar, and every one of them turned to look at Steve.

He swallowed. He thought about Kevin back on the shore, probably crying, definitely holding the bow wrong. He thought about item seven, and how easily it could have said *cremation, nice urn, somewhere on the mantel.*

Steve raised his stick.

"Okay," he said. "Before we start — does anyone want to talk about this?"

Nobody did.

Do Young People Respect Their Elders Less Today?

It's common to hear adults say that "kids these days" don't respect older people. My grandmother says it, and I've heard teachers say it too. I can see why some people believe this, but I don't fully agree. I think young people still respect older generations. We just show it differently, and sometimes the generations misunderstand each other.

People who believe respect is declining usually point to manners. Teenagers today might not say "sir" or "ma'am," they might keep looking at their phones when an adult is talking, and they may argue with parents or teachers instead of quietly obeying. On social media, jokes like "OK, boomer" can make it seem like young people dismiss everything older people say. I'll admit some of this behavior is genuinely rude, and my generation could do better at things like putting our phones away during conversations.

However, I think much of what looks like disrespect is really a change in culture. Society as a whole has become more casual. My parents call their bosses by their first names, something their own parents would never have done. Also, schools today encourage us to ask questions and think for ourselves. When a student politely disagrees with a teacher, it can come across as disrespect, but often it just means the student is engaged and thinking critically.

Young people also show respect in ways that are easy to miss. Many teenagers I know help their grandparents with technology, like setting up a new phone or showing them how to video call relatives. Others help care for older family members or volunteer at senior centers. In my own family, I take my grandfather to his weekly checkers club because he can't drive anymore. Those actions show real respect, even if they don't look like the old-fashioned kind.

Respect also has to go both ways. Teenagers are more likely to respect adults who listen to them and take their opinions seriously. When older people dismiss young people as lazy or entitled, it creates a cycle where neither side feels respected.

In conclusion, I don't believe young people today have less respect for older generations. The way we show respect has changed, becoming less formal and more personal, but it is still there. If both generations spend more time understanding each other instead of complaining, they will see that respect never really disappeared.

Deep inelastic scattering measurements at the HERA electron–proton collider provide the most precise determination of proton structure over a wide kinematic domain. This paper reviews the measurement of the neutral- and charged-current structure functions F₂, F_L and xF₃ by the H1 and ZEUS collaborations, covering four-momentum transfers from below 1 GeV² to above 10⁴ GeV² and Bjorken x down to approximately 10⁻⁶. The procedure for combining the two experiments' data sets, including the treatment of correlated systematic uncertainties, is described, together with its application in the HERAPDF next-to-leading and next-to-next-to-leading order QCD analyses. The resulting parton distribution functions constrain the valence, sea and gluon densities, with particular sensitivity to the gluon at low x. Implications for precision predictions at the LHC and the remaining theoretical uncertainties are discussed.

**Abstract**

We study moduli stabilisation in type II orientifold compactifications on the T^6/(Z_2 × Z_2) orbifold in the presence of general flux backgrounds, including gauge, geometric and non-geometric fluxes. The resulting four-dimensional theories are N = 1 supergravities whose superpotentials depend polynomially on all closed-string moduli, with flux parameters constrained by Bianchi identities and tadpole cancellation conditions. We show that the Bianchi identities can be recast as the Jacobi identities of an underlying gauge algebra of the effective supergravity, so that the space of consistent flux configurations can be organised algebraically. Exploiting this correspondence, we classify the admissible algebras and analyse the vacuum structure associated with each. We derive no-go theorems that forbid de Sitter, and in certain cases Minkowski, vacua with all moduli stabilised for specific classes of algebras, and identify the algebraic structures capable of evading these restrictions. Our results clarify the interplay between duality-covariant fluxes, gauge algebras and vacuum selection in string compactifications.

The Israeli–Palestinian conflict is a long-standing dispute between Israelis and Palestinians over land, sovereignty, security, and national identity in the territory between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.

**Origins.** In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, Jewish nationalism (Zionism) and Arab Palestinian nationalism both developed claims to the same land, which was then under Ottoman and later British rule. Jewish immigration grew, and tensions with the Arab population increased. In 1947 the United Nations proposed partitioning the territory into Jewish and Arab states. Jewish leaders accepted the plan, and Arab leaders rejected it.

**1948 and after.** Israel declared independence in 1948, and a war followed with neighboring Arab states. Roughly 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, an event Palestinians call the *Nakba* ("catastrophe"). In the 1967 war, Israel captured the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip, among other territories.

**Core issues.** The central disputes include:
- **Borders** and the possible creation of a Palestinian state
- **Israeli settlements** in the West Bank
- **The status of Jerusalem**, which both peoples claim as a capital
- **Palestinian refugees** and their descendants
- **Security** for Israelis, who face rocket fire and attacks, and for Palestinians, who live under military occupation and restrictions

**Recent developments.** Peace efforts, most notably the Oslo Accords of the 1990s, have not produced a final settlement. The Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, and the war in Gaza that followed caused severe loss of life and a major humanitarian crisis. The conflict remains unresolved.

Christopher Columbus reached the Americas in **1492**. On **October 12, 1492**, his expedition made landfall on an island in the Bahamas. The native Lucayan people called it Guanahani, and Columbus renamed it San Salvador. Historians still disagree about exactly which modern island it was, though today's San Salvador Island is the traditional candidate.

### How the voyage came about

Columbus was a Genoese navigator who spent years seeking a sponsor for a westward route to Asia. He believed the ocean between Europe and the Indies was much narrower than it really is. This was a serious miscalculation: he underestimated both the size of the Earth and the distance to Asia. The Portuguese crown turned him down. So did others. Eventually, after the fall of Granada in early 1492, Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain agreed to back him. The terms, set out in the Capitulations of Santa Fe, promised him titles, governorship of any lands he found, and a share of the profits.

### The first voyage

Columbus left Palos de la Frontera on **August 3, 1492**, with three ships: the *Santa María*, the *Pinta* and the *Niña*. After stopping in the Canary Islands for repairs and supplies, the fleet headed west in early September. The crossing took about five weeks. Crew morale became shaky as time went on, and Columbus reportedly kept two logs so his men would think they hadn't gone as far as they actually had.

In the early hours of October 12, a lookout on the *Pinta*, Rodrigo de Triana, sighted land. After landing in the Bahamas, Columbus sailed on to Cuba and then Hispaniola, the island now shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic. On Christmas Eve the *Santa María* ran aground off Hispaniola. Using its timbers, Columbus built a small settlement called La Navidad and left about 39 men there before heading back to Spain in early 1493.

### Later voyages

Columbus made three more voyages:

- **1493–1496:** A large colonizing expedition. He found La Navidad destroyed and its men dead.
- **1498–1500:** He reached the coast of South America, near the Orinoco River in present-day Venezuela. This was his first landing on the American mainland.
- **1502–1504:** He explored the coast of Central America, including present-day Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama.

To the end of his life he insisted he had reached the outskirts of Asia. He died in Valladolid, Spain, in 1506.

### Important context

Columbus was not the first European to reach the Americas. Norse explorers led by Leif Erikson arrived around the year 1000, and archaeologists have confirmed a Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland. And millions of Indigenous people had already been living throughout the Americas for thousands of years.

What made 1492 a turning point was what came afterward. Columbus's voyages started lasting contact between Europe and the Americas, which led to the Columbian Exchange of plants, animals and diseases, and to colonization. The consequences for Indigenous peoples were devastating, including enslavement, violence and catastrophic population loss from disease. That is why the date matters so much historically, and also why its legacy is still debated today.

Your taste preferences were shaped for a world of scarcity. For most of human history, sugar, fat, and salt were hard to come by and extremely valuable: sugar meant quick energy from ripe fruit, fat packed the most calories into every bite, and salt was essential for nerve and muscle function. People who craved them were more likely to survive, so our brains evolved to reward those flavors with pleasure. Meanwhile, the bitterness common in many vegetables often signaled toxins, so we're naturally wary of it.

Today those once-rare nutrients are cheap and everywhere, and food companies deliberately combine them in proportions designed to be irresistible. The cravings stayed; the scarcity didn't.

**Palmer Understanding as Woods Skips Bay Hill in Race to Be Ready for Augusta**

ORLANDO, Fla. — Arnold Palmer says he holds no hard feelings about Tiger Woods skipping this week's Arnold Palmer Invitational, acknowledging that the former world No. 1 has bigger concerns as he tries to get his game in shape for next month's Masters.

Woods, an eight-time winner at Bay Hill Club & Lodge, did not enter the tournament, leaving the event without one of its most reliable draws. Speaking to reporters at the club, Palmer said he understood the decision and that Woods needed to do what was best for his health and his game.

The 85-year-old tournament host said he had been in touch with Woods and believed the 14-time major champion was working hard to return, adding that he hoped to see him back at Bay Hill in the years ahead.

Woods has not played competitively since early February, when he withdrew from the Farmers Insurance Open at Torrey Pines after 11 holes, citing tightness in his lower back. A week earlier, he shot an 82 at the Waste Management Phoenix Open, the worst score of his professional career, and missed the cut.

After the withdrawal, Woods announced he would step away from tournament golf until his game was good enough to compete at the highest level. He has been practicing near his home in Jupiter, Fla., but has offered few public details about his progress.

The struggles have been most visible around the greens. In his brief appearances this season, Woods repeatedly chunked and bladed short chip shots, a startling sight for a player once regarded as one of the finest short-game artists in history. He has attributed some of the problems to the transition between swing patterns under new consultant Chris Como.

That leaves his Masters participation in doubt. Woods, a four-time champion at Augusta National, missed last year's tournament after undergoing back surgery on March 31, 2014, the first time he had sat out the Masters as a professional. He has indicated he will play only if he believes he can contend.

Palmer, who won four green jackets himself, said he would like nothing more than to see Woods at Augusta, but cautioned that rushing back could do more damage than staying away a little longer.

The absence is a familiar one for Bay Hill. Woods also missed last year's edition while recovering from his back injury. Before that, he dominated the event, winning four straight times from 2000 to 2003 and adding titles in 2008, 2009, 2012 and 2013.

Tournament officials have stressed that the field remains strong without him, with several of the world's top players in Orlando to fine-tune their preparations for the season's first major.

Still, Woods' absence underlines the uncertainty surrounding a player who has not won a major since the 2008 U.S. Open. Now 39, he has tumbled down the world rankings and faces mounting questions about whether he can recapture the form that once made him the dominant figure in the sport.

The Masters begins April 9. Woods has until shortly before the tournament to decide whether he will tee it up.

Quantifying how information is distributed across the components of a multivariate system remains a central open problem in information theory, with direct consequences for neuroscience, complex systems, and machine learning. The Partial Information Decomposition (PID) addresses part of this problem by splitting the mutual information that a set of predictor variables carries about a target into redundant, unique, and synergistic contributions. However, the PID treats predictors and target asymmetrically, and no measure of redundancy has yet gained general acceptance. In this paper, we apply the lattice formalism of the PID directly to the joint entropy of a set of variables, yielding a Partial Entropy Decomposition (PED) that treats all variables symmetrically. We define redundant entropy through pointwise common surprisal, the positive overlap between the local surprisals of individual variables for each joint outcome, averaged over the distribution; this mirrors the definition of mutual information as expected shared surprisal. We show that the PED distinguishes dyadic from triadic dependency structures in systems whose classical Shannon quantities are identical. The decomposition also reveals that mutual information is not a purely redundant quantity: pointwise misinformation appears as synergistic entropy, so mutual information contains both redundant and synergistic components. Using the relationship between the PED and mutual information for two predictors, we derive two alternative information decompositions and illustrate them on canonical examples. These results show that, in entropy terms, the information carried by a single predictor is not a proper subset of the joint information, which may partly explain why consistent PID measures have proved difficult to construct. Finally, the PED allows mechanistic redundancy to be quantified separately from redundancy arising from dependencies among the inputs.

**Banning Single-Use Plastics: A Necessary Step**

Governments should ban most single-use plastic products. Items like plastic bags, straws, cutlery, and takeaway containers are used for minutes but can last for centuries. Only a small fraction of plastic is ever recycled. The rest piles up in landfills, gets burned, or washes into rivers and oceans, where it harms wildlife and breaks down into microplastics that now turn up in drinking water and human blood.

Voluntary efforts have not been enough, because convenience usually wins. Bans work: after countries such as Kenya and Rwanda prohibited plastic bags, litter dropped sharply and reusable alternatives quickly became normal.

A ban should be designed carefully, though. Exemptions are needed for medical supplies and for people with disabilities who rely on items such as bendable straws. Governments should also phase bans in gradually so businesses can adapt. With those safeguards, banning single-use plastics is a practical and overdue policy.

**Is It Ethical to Use Animals in Scientific Research?**

Every year, millions of animals such as mice, rats, and monkeys are used in scientific research. This practice has helped create many medicines and treatments, but it also raises serious moral questions. In my opinion, using animals in research can be ethical, but only under strict conditions.

On one hand, animal research has saved countless human lives. Vaccines for diseases like polio, treatments for diabetes, and many surgical techniques were developed with the help of animal studies. Scientists argue that before a new drug is given to people, it must be tested on a living body to make sure it is safe. Testing directly on humans would be far more dangerous and unethical.

On the other hand, animals can feel pain, stress, and fear just like humans can. Many people believe it is wrong to make them suffer for our benefit, especially when they cannot give consent. In addition, animals do not always react to drugs the same way humans do, so some experiments may not even give useful results. This makes their suffering seem even harder to justify.

Because both sides have strong points, I believe the best approach is a balanced one. Animal research should only be allowed when there is no other option and when the goal is truly important, such as curing a serious disease. Scientists should follow the "Three Rs": replace animals with other methods whenever possible, reduce the number of animals used, and refine experiments to cause less pain. New technologies, like computer models and lab-grown tissues, may also help lower the need for animal testing in the future.

In conclusion, animal research is not simply right or wrong. It can be ethical if it is done carefully, responsibly, and with respect for the animals involved.

When an investor turned down Jia Jiang's startup idea in 2012, the rejection hurt so much that he nearly abandoned his dream of becoming an entrepreneur. Instead, he decided to get used to hearing "no."

Jiang, who moved from China to the United States as a teenager, gave himself a challenge: every day for 100 days, he would make a request he expected to be refused, and he would film each attempt.

The requests were deliberately unusual. He asked a stranger to lend him $100. He asked a burger restaurant for a "burger refill." He asked to play soccer in a stranger's backyard.

Then, on day three, he walked into a Krispy Kreme and asked for doughnuts linked together like the Olympic rings. To his astonishment, the employee made them. The video spread rapidly online, drawing millions of views, and "100 Days of Rejection" suddenly had a global audience.

What began as personal therapy turned into an unexpected career. Jiang wrote a book, "Rejection Proof," delivered a popular TED talk and now speaks to audiences about overcoming fear.

The experiment pushed him far outside his comfort zone, but it taught him that rejection itself is rarely as painful as people imagine. What really holds us back, Jiang concluded, is the fear of rejection — the dread of hearing "no" that keeps many people from asking at all.

Along the way, he discovered something else: when he asked, people said "yes" far more often than he expected.

**Chilean Teenager With Cystic Fibrosis Asks President for Right to Die**

SANTIAGO, Chile — A 14-year-old girl suffering from cystic fibrosis has appealed directly to President Michelle Bachelet for permission to end her life, prompting a national debate over euthanasia in a country where assisted suicide remains illegal.

In a video posted online, Valentina Maureira, speaking from a hospital bed, addresses the president calmly. "I urgently request to speak with the President because I am tired of living with this illness," she says. "She can authorize the injection that will make me sleep forever."

Cystic fibrosis is a hereditary disease that causes thick mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system, leading to severe respiratory infections and progressive organ damage. There is no cure, and treatment, which typically involves daily physiotherapy, medication and frequent hospital stays, can be physically exhausting. According to her family, Valentina's older brother died of the same disease when he was a young child.

Her father, Freddy Maureira, told local media that his daughter's request had come as a surprise but that the family would support her wishes. He said she had grown weary of repeated hospital admissions and invasive procedures.

The government responded within days. A spokesperson for the presidency stated that the president could not grant the request, noting that Chilean law does not permit euthanasia or assisted suicide. Officials expressed sympathy for the family and said the government would ensure the girl received all available medical and psychological support.

President Bachelet, herself a trained pediatrician, later visited Valentina at the hospital. Details of the private meeting were not disclosed.

The appeal has reignited discussion in the Chilean Congress, where proposals to legalize euthanasia under strict conditions have previously been introduced without success. Supporters argue that patients with terminal, incurable illnesses should be allowed to choose a dignified death. Opponents, including representatives of the Roman Catholic Church, which retains considerable influence in Chile, maintain that legalizing the practice would undermine the protection of human life and could place pressure on vulnerable patients.

Medical ethicists have also emphasized the particular complexity of the case because of Valentina's age. Even in the few countries that permit euthanasia for minors, such as Belgium and the Netherlands, strict requirements apply regarding parental consent and assessments of the child's capacity to make such a decision.

Valentina remains in hospital, where she continues to receive treatment.

Cuteness is subjective, but a few animals show up on almost everyone's list:

- **Red panda**: Fluffy, ringed tail, a face like a living teddy bear, and a habit of standing up on its hind legs when startled.
- **Quokka**: A small Australian marsupial known as "the happiest animal in the world" because its face looks like it's always smiling.
- **Sea otter**: Holds hands with other otters while sleeping so they don't drift apart.
- **Fennec fox**: A tiny desert fox with enormous ears.
- **Pygmy hippo**: A round, shiny miniature of the regular hippo. Moo Deng made them internet-famous.
- **Slow loris**: Huge eyes and a permanently surprised look. Beware, though: it's one of the few venomous mammals.
- **Axolotl**: A salamander with frilly gills and a goofy grin.
- **Penguin chicks**: Fuzzy and clumsy, which makes them endlessly charming.

Honorable mentions go to baby elephants, pikas, and the Japanese dwarf flying squirrel.

Films and television series can be highly effective tools for improving English, as they expose learners to authentic pronunciation, natural vocabulary and cultural context. The following selections are organized by proficiency level.

**Beginner to Lower Intermediate**

- **Friends** (TV series): The dialogue is conversational, the situations are everyday, and the episodes are short. Its popularity also means transcripts are widely available.
- **Peppa Pig** or **Bluey** (animated series): Although intended for children, these programs use clear pronunciation and simple sentence structures, making them useful for absolute beginners.
- **Paddington** (2014) and **Paddington 2** (2017): Gentle, well-paced films with clear British English and uncomplicated plots.

**Intermediate**

- **Modern Family** (TV series): Presents a variety of speaking styles and accents within realistic family situations.
- **The Devil Wears Prada** (2006): Introduces workplace and professional vocabulary in an accessible narrative.
- **Ted Lasso** (TV series): Contrasts American and British English and features expressive, well-articulated dialogue.

**Upper Intermediate to Advanced**

- **The Crown** (TV series): Offers formal British English and historical and political vocabulary.
- **Suits** (TV series): Rich in legal and business terminology delivered at a brisk pace.
- **The Social Network** (2010): Fast, dense dialogue that provides a demanding but rewarding listening exercise.

**Recommendations for Effective Use**

1. Begin with subtitles in your native language, then switch to English subtitles, and eventually remove them altogether.
2. Rewatch short scenes and repeat lines aloud to practice pronunciation and intonation.
3. Record unfamiliar expressions in a notebook and review them regularly.
4. Prioritize consistency: watching twenty minutes daily is generally more effective than occasional long sessions.

The judge read the sentence the way judges always do, without looking up. "Life imprisonment, without the possibility of parole."

Elias Varn, who had been born in a village that no longer appeared on any map, allowed himself a small smile. His lawyer elbowed him. It was not, she whispered, a good look.

He served his first forty years quietly. He worked in the laundry, then the library, then the laundry again when a new warden decided the library was a privilege. He learned the names of the guards and then the names of their children, who eventually became guards themselves. He did not age, which the prison handled the way institutions handle most impossible things: by losing the paperwork.

In year sixty-three, a young man from the state auditor's office came to see him.

"According to our records," the auditor said, flipping through a binder, "you're one hundred and four years old."

"Older," Elias said. "But I wouldn't put that in the report."

"You look thirty."

"I moisturize."

The auditor did not laugh. He explained, with growing distress, that the sentence was for life, that Elias's life appeared to have no end, and that the state had not budgeted for infinity.

"I could leave," Elias offered.

"You can't. You were sentenced to life."

"Then I suppose we're stuck with each other."

The prison closed in year one hundred and twelve. They moved him to a new facility with automated doors and meals delivered by robot. In year two hundred and five, the country that had convicted him split into three smaller countries, none of which wanted to inherit an immortal inmate. Lawyers argued for a decade. Elias stayed put, reading.

In year four hundred, the last human guard retired. The building kept running on its own: lights on at six, off at ten, meals at regular intervals. Elias still swept his cell every morning.

One day the door simply opened. A power failure, maybe, or a glitch that no one remained to fix. Sunlight lay across the threshold like a carpet.

Elias looked at it for a long time.

Then he picked up his book, found his place, and kept reading. The sentence wasn't finished. He had always been a man who kept his word, and he had nothing but time to keep it.

**Lost and Found**

The first thing I found was a red umbrella, half-buried in the sand above the tide line. I knew it was mine before I'd even pulled it free. I'd left it on a streetcar in Toronto in 2009, and here was the same bent spoke, the same coffee ring on the handle.

I didn't think much about it. I had bigger problems: no boat, no radio, and a coastline that curved away in both directions without a single sign of another person. So I did what the survival shows tell you to do. I went looking for supplies.

Within an hour I'd found my Swiss Army knife, the one I lost at summer camp when I was eleven, my initials still scratched into the red casing. Then a green lighter. Then the sleeping bag I'd abandoned at a music festival, a tarp, a thermos, and an alarming number of water bottles. By noon I had a pile of gear that would have made a quartermaster weep.

I also had forty-three pairs of sunglasses. I had not realized it was forty-three.

Behind the dunes was a hollow filled with nothing but socks. Single socks, thousands of them, every color I'd ever owned, drifted against the palm trunks like snow. I sat down in them and laughed until it turned into something else.

That was when I started to understand the rules. The island didn't hold everything — only the things that had been mine and then weren't. Keys. Library cards. The retainer my parents paid for twice. A ten-dollar bill I dropped outside a movie theater in 1997, still folded into quarters. My grandmother's ring, which I lost when I moved apartments and told my mother had been stolen. I held that one for a long time.

On the second day, a dog came out of the trees.

She was small and brown, with one ear that never stood up, and she ran at me the way she used to when I came home from school. Biscuit. She'd slipped her collar when I was nine, and we'd covered the neighborhood in posters and never heard a thing. She hadn't aged a day. Lost things, apparently, wait exactly as you left them.

I cried into her fur, and she licked the salt off my face, and for a while I didn't care about being rescued at all.

But the longer I walked, the more I wondered what else was out there. I had lost things that weren't shaped like things. A friend named Marcus I'd simply stopped calling. Most of my twenties. The version of me who sang in the car and believed things would work out because they usually had. If he was anywhere, he'd be here.

On the third morning I climbed the island's only hill to look for him.

He wasn't there. But below me, on the far shore, rocking in the shallows with its anchor line trailing, was the boat I had lost three days earlier.

Of course. Everything.

I spent the afternoon deciding what to take. The boat was small. I couldn't bring forty-three pairs of sunglasses or a dune of socks, and I left the ten-dollar bill on a rock for whoever washed up next. Marcus wasn't on the island anywhere, and neither was the version of me who sang in the car. I decided that meant they weren't lost. I'd just stopped going back for them.

I took water. I took the knife. I took my grandmother's ring, because I owed my mother a phone call and the truth.

And I took the dog, who leapt into the bow before I could ask, as though she'd spent twenty-six years waiting for someone to come and bring her home.
